topic: Ornith 1.5 9B: a frontier-level SWE-bench score out of a four-bit build that fits a mid-range gaming card
title: Ornith 1.5 9B: 70.6 from a 6 GB file
description:
Ornith 1.5 9B and the 6 GB file: a frontier-level score without frontier hardware.

Ornith reports 70.6 on SWE-bench Verified for a 9B dense model whose four-bit GGUF build is 5.63 GB on disk. That is small enough for the mid-range gaming card already in your machine, which is where the "frontier score needs frontier hardware" rule stops holding. The catch is that the numbers are Ornith's own, averaged over five runs with the git history stripped and network access disabled.

You'll learn: what the four-bit build actually weighs, what SWE-bench Verified measures, how Ornith ran the evaluation, and the one place the myth still holds.

Model card: https://huggingface.co/ornith-ai/Ornith-1.5-9B-GGUF

Subscribe for more local AI builds. (Narration is AI-generated.)

narration_full: You have been told a frontier score needs frontier hardware. This one is under six gigabytes on disk. That's Ornith's four-bit build, where every stored number keeps fewer bits. It fits the mid-range gaming card you already own, with room to spare. Ornith reports seventy point six on the verified benchmark for fixing real bugs in real repositories. Ornith ran those numbers itself, averaged over five runs, with the git history stripped and the network off. Stricter than most labs, and still their own. The myth survives on knowledge, not on hardware. A nine-billion-parameter model still will not know what a much bigger one knows.

notes_for_review: Four key numbers spent: the four-bit file size, the SWE-bench Verified score, the five averaged runs and the parameter count in the payoff.
